title: Hall Burger Bar
shortDescription: Smash burgers with toppings bar for ten
subtitle: Smash burgers with toppings bar for ten
description: Loose 3-ounce balls of 80/20 chuck smashed paper-thin on a screaming-hot flat-top for a lacy brown crust, finished with American cheese and oven bacon. The toppings bar rides on the side so every firefighter builds their own double.
equipment: Hotel pans for the toppings bar

ingredients.name: ground beef (80/20)
ingredients.notes: sixteen 3-oz balls — two patties per firefighter

ingredients.name: burger buns
ingredients.notes: doubles use one bun; extras for second-round singles

steps.title: Bake the bacon on racks
steps.instruction: Lay bacon strips on wire racks over foil-lined sheet pans and slide into a 400°F oven for 18–20 minutes until deep mahogany and rigid when you lift a strip. Racks let the fat drip away so the strips crisp instead of stewing flat in grease. Don't chase an internal temp here — crisp bacon is far past safe long before it crunches. Drain on paper towels; it keeps firming as it cools.

steps.title: Slice out the toppings bar
steps.instruction: While the bacon bakes, shred the iceberg lettuce fine, slice the beefsteak tomatoes a quarter-inch thick, and cut the red onion into thin rings. Load lettuce, tomatoes, onion, and dill pickle chips into labeled hotel pans and portion ketchup and mustard into squeeze bottles or bowls. Hold off salting the tomato slices until service — salt pulls their water out and floods the pan within 15 minutes.

steps.title: Portion loose beef balls
steps.instruction: Divide the ground beef into sixteen 3-ounce balls with the lightest touch you can manage — roll each just enough to hold together, about 5 minutes of work. Compacted meat fights the smash and cooks up dense instead of craggy. Keep the balls cold on a sheet pan in the fridge until the flat-top is ready; cold, loose beef smashes cleaner and holds onto its fat.

steps.title: Get the flat-top ripping hot
steps.instruction: Set the griddle or two cast-iron skillets over high heat for a full 5–8 minutes — a drop of water flicked on the surface should bead up and skate off almost instantly, which means roughly 450–500°F. A merely warm surface is the number one smash-burger failure: the patty turns gray and steams instead of building a brown crust. Turn on the hood fan and crack a window; real smash burgers make smoke.

steps.title: Smash hard within ten seconds
steps.instruction: Drop 4–6 balls onto the hot surface with space between them, then immediately press each one dead flat with a stiff spatula — stack the second spatula on top for leverage. You have about ten seconds before the crust starts setting; after that, pressing squeezes out juice instead of building surface. Thin, ragged edges are the goal. Season the smashed patties with kosher salt while the first side cooks, about 2 minutes, until the edges go deep brown and lacy.

steps.title: Scrape, flip, and cheese
steps.instruction: Work the spatula edge fully under each patty and scrape hard — the crust is bonded to the steel, and a timid flip leaves the best part behind. Flip, lay a slice of American cheese on every patty, and cook about 1 minute more. Patties this thin blow past the 160°F ground-beef safe mark almost instantly — spot-check one from each batch with an instant-read thermometer and it will read well over. Pull to a sheet pan and repeat with the remaining balls.

steps.title: Toast buns in the drippings
steps.instruction: Scrape most of the fat off one zone of the surface, then press the burger buns cut-side down for 30–60 seconds until golden at the edges. Toasting in the drippings adds flavor and, more important, waterproofs the crumb so the bun survives juicy patties and ketchup without collapsing. Work in waves timed to each patty batch so buns and meat land hot together.

steps.title: Stack doubles and call the crew
steps.instruction: Build the first pass as doubles: bottom bun, patty, cheese, patty, bacon, then lettuce, tomato, onion, and pickles from the bar. Keep the hot patties and buns together near the flat-top with the cold toppings pans at the far end, and call the crew within 5 minutes — a smash patty holds its crust maybe ten minutes before it softens.

steps.title: Hold for call interruptions
steps.instruction: If tones drop mid-cook: turn off direct heat and cover the smash patties — hold at 140°F in a warm cabinet or 200°F oven, never below 140°F for more than 30 minutes cumulative. Log hold time on the pan with a grease pencil. If tones drop after service, cover hot food and keep sides on low heat or ice as appropriate. On return, spot-check proteins at safe internal temp before reopening the line.

steps.title: Pack down leftovers safely
steps.instruction: Cool smash patties and hot components in shallow hotel pans within two hours — deep pots stay in the danger zone too long. Label with date; reheat proteins to 165°F minimum before second shift. Store cold components separately so textures survive overnight.

proTips: Roll the beef balls the night before and refrigerate — cold, loose-packed balls smash cleaner and hold together on the flat-top.
If raw beef grabs the spatula, smash through a square of parchment: press, peel, season.
Smash means smash — put real body weight into the press. A gentle pat gives you a meatball with a crust ring, not a lacy patty.
One cheese slice on the patty and one on the top bun doubles the melt without extra time on the heat.
Keep a backup tray at 200°F for firefighters returning from a run — never serve picked-over pans to late crew.
Taste for salt at the end — hall palates run salty after long shifts.
Log hold times on the pan with a grease pencil when tones drop mid-service.
Spot-check proteins with an instant-read thermometer before reopening the line after a call.
tonightSpread: Main: Double smash burgers with oven bacon
Sides: oven fries or tater tots if the hall votes for them
Condiments: ketchup, mustard, dill pickles, shredded lettuce, tomato, red onion
Set hot components closest to the crew; cold crunch and toppings at the far end of the line.
Keep a backup tray at 200°F for firefighters returning from a run.
leftovers: Cool smash patties in shallow pans within two hours; label with date and reheat to 165°F before second shift.
Store cold sides separately — hot and cold stacked overnight ruins texture.
Day-two patties revive best in a hot dry pan, 1 minute per side — the microwave turns that crust to rubber.
Chop extra patties into cheeseburger mac or a breakfast hash with the leftover bar onions.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Doubles built to order with real diner crust — the smash press is the most fought-over job in the kitchen, and the pickles-no-onions crowd and the double-bacon crowd both leave happy.
mealPrepNotes: Form loose 3-ounce balls ahead and refrigerate on a sheet pan. Pre-slice all toppings into hotel pans. Bacon bakes on racks while the flat-top heats, so everything lands at once.
substitutions: Ground turkey swaps in but runs lean — film the surface with a tablespoon of oil per batch and expect less crust.
No griddle? Two cast-iron skillets side by side keep batches moving; nonstick can't take this heat and won't build crust.
Sharp cheddar works instead of American — add it right at the flip and cap with a pan lid for 30 seconds so it melts in time.
Brioche or potato rolls swap for standard buns; softer crumb, so toast them a touch longer.
